author: A Robot
objectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.
Explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to pressure demands.
Describe how atrioventricular and semilunar valves prevent backflow and identify what each valve separates.

modules.description: Side-by-side intact and cutaway heart models introduce anatomical orientation, patient right-left perspective, the apex, and major vessel landmarks.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Orient the heart with apex inferior and toward the patient's left.
Distinguish anatomical right and left from the viewer's perspective.
Compare exterior great vessels with the cutaway view of internal anatomy.
instructions: Place the models on a tabletop surface within arm's reach.
Advance through the clips to reveal orientation cues.
Remember that right and left are named from the patient's perspective.

components.text: Heart Orientation: Exterior + Cutaway
Patient RIGHT
Patient LEFT

clips.changeMeaning: The intact and cutaway hearts are shown side by side to establish that students will compare exterior landmarks with internal anatomy throughout the lab.
clips.narration: We begin with two views of the same human heart. The intact model shows the external surface and great vessels. The cutaway model removes the anterior wall so the chambers and valves are visible.

clips.changeMeaning: Patient right and left labels appear beside the cutaway heart to correct the common viewer-perspective misconception.
clips.narration: Heart anatomy is named from the patient's perspective. When you face the model, the patient's right heart appears on your left, and the patient's left heart appears on your right.

clips.changeMeaning: The apex arrow appears and the model rotates slightly to emphasize the apex direction and the superior great vessel region.
clips.narration: The apex points downward and toward the patient's left. At the superior aspect, the aorta, pulmonary trunk, venae cavae, and pulmonary veins form the major entry and exit routes.

modules.description: A sequential structural tour highlights chambers, valves, and major vessels on a cutaway heart while matching each internal highlight to an exterior landmark.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the four heart chambers in anatomical context.
Identify the four valves and state what each separates.
Identify superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta.
Map internal structures to exterior landmarks on the intact heart.
instructions: Advance in order through chambers, valves, and vessels.
Compare the internal highlight on the cutaway heart with the exterior highlight on the intact model.
Read each label aloud for vocabulary reinforcement.

components.text: Structural tour

Right atrium + right ventricle
Deoxygenated side

clips.changeMeaning: The highlights focus on the right atrium and right ventricle, introducing the deoxygenated side of the heart and its lung-directed pump.
clips.narration: Start with the right atrium, which receives systemic venous blood. Below it, the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood toward the pulmonary circuit.

components.text:
Left atrium + left ventricle
Oxygenated side

clips.changeMeaning: The highlights shift to the left atrium and left ventricle, contrasting oxygenated pulmonary venous return with systemic ejection.
clips.narration: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins. The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta for systemic circulation.

components.text:
Valves:
Tricuspid • Pulmonary
Mitral/Bicuspid • Aortic

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight shrinks to the valve plane, emphasizing valves as one-way gates between chambers or from ventricles into arteries.
clips.narration: Now locate the valves. Tricuspid is between right atrium and right ventricle. Pulmonary is between right ventricle and pulmonary trunk. Mitral, or bicuspid, is between left atrium and left ventricle. Aortic is between left ventricle and aorta.

components.text:
Great vessels:
SVC • IVC • Pulmonary arteries
Pulmonary veins • Aorta

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight elongates over the superior great vessel region to shift from chamber-valve anatomy to entry and exit vessel routes.
clips.narration: Finally, identify the major vessels: superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta. These vessels define the routes into and out of the heart.

modules.description: Blue and red flow streams clarify deoxygenated and oxygenated blood patterns and distinguish pulmonary and systemic loops.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Associate blue flow with deoxygenated blood and red flow with oxygenated blood in the instructional model.
Explain that the right heart pumps to the lungs and the left heart pumps to the body.
Distinguish pulmonary and systemic circuits as two linked loops.
instructions: Observe both colored streams before reading the labels.
Notice that pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.
Advance to isolate the pulmonary and systemic loops separately.

components.text:
Pulmonary circuit:
right heart → lungs → left heart

Systemic circuit:
left heart → body → right heart

clips.changeMeaning: Blue and red flow streams appear in the translucent cutaway to establish oxygenation as a visual code for the rest of the lab.
clips.narration: This model uses blue for deoxygenated blood and red for oxygenated blood. The right side of the heart handles deoxygenated blood, and the left side handles oxygenated blood.

clips.changeMeaning: The pulmonary label and ring appear around the right-heart-to-lung loop, separating it from the systemic loop.
clips.narration: The pulmonary circuit sends deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, then returns oxygenated blood through pulmonary veins to the left atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight shifts to the left-heart-to-body loop, contrasting systemic circulation with the shorter pulmonary circuit.
clips.narration: The systemic circuit sends oxygenated blood from the left ventricle through the aorta to the body. Venous blood then returns to the right atrium through the venae cavae.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Step-by-Step Red Blood Cell Trace
modules.description: A single enlarged blood cell advances through the complete route from vena cava to right heart, lungs, left heart, aorta, body, and back to the veins.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Sequence the complete pathway of blood through chambers, valves, vessels, lungs, and systemic tissues.
Describe oxygenation change in lung capillaries and deoxygenation at systemic tissues.
Recognize the valves encountered during the one-way pathway.
instructions: Press Next to move the cell step by step.
Read each structure label and connect it to the previous and next structures.
Replay the trace until you can state the entire pathway without prompts.

components.text: Start: Superior vena cava
1. Right atrium

clips.changeMeaning: The blue blood cell moves from the superior vena cava into the right atrium, beginning systemic venous return.
clips.narration: A unit of deoxygenated blood returns from the body through the superior vena cava and enters the right atrium.

components.text: 2. Tricuspid valve → Right ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: The cell descends through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, demonstrating the right atrioventricular transition.
clips.narration: The right atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

components.text: 3. Pulmonary valve → Pulmonary arteries → Lungs

clips.changeMeaning: The cell travels through the pulmonary outflow route to the lungs, highlighting that pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood.
clips.narration: The right ventricle contracts, sending the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries, then to lung capillaries.

components.text:
4. Pulmonary veins → Left atrium
oxygenated blood

clips.changeMeaning: The cell changes from blue to red after lung gas exchange and moves through pulmonary venous return into the left atrium.
clips.narration: In the lung capillaries, the cell picks up oxygen and becomes oxygenated. It returns through pulmonary veins and enters the left atrium.

components.text: 5. Mitral valve → Left ventricle → Aortic valve → Aorta

clips.changeMeaning: The red cell travels through the mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, and aorta to represent systemic outflow.
clips.narration: The left atrium sends the cell through the mitral, or bicuspid, valve into the left ventricle. The left ventricle ejects it through the aortic valve into the aorta.

components.text: 6. Systemic tissues → Systemic veins → Venae cavae

clips.changeMeaning: The cell completes systemic circulation, changes back to blue after oxygen delivery, and returns to the venous entry route.
clips.narration: From the aorta, blood travels to systemic tissues. After oxygen delivery, it becomes deoxygenated and returns through systemic veins to the venae cavae.

modules.description: Matched ventricular cross-sections compare the thin right ventricular myocardium with the thicker left ventricular myocardium and connect form to pressure demands.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare typical right and left ventricular myocardial wall thicknesses.
Relate wall thickness to low-pressure pulmonary versus high-pressure systemic circulation.
Use scale markers to support the approximate three-to-one thickness relationship.
instructions: Rotate the comparison if desired.
Compare the highlighted myocardial bands to the scale marker.
Connect the thickness difference to the pressure each ventricle must generate.

components.text:
Right ventricle
~3–5 mm wall

Left ventricle
~10–15 mm wall

clips.changeMeaning: Two cross-sections appear at comparable ventricular levels so students can make a fair visual comparison of wall thickness.
clips.narration: These cross-sections show the ventricles at comparable levels. The right ventricle is on the left, and the left ventricle is on the right.

clips.changeMeaning: The right ventricular wall is highlighted and labeled with a typical healthy adult thickness range linked to pulmonary circulation.
clips.narration: The right ventricle has a thinner myocardium, about three to five millimeters in a healthy adult, because it pumps only to the nearby low-pressure lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: The left ventricular wall highlight appears, showing substantially thicker myocardium for high-pressure systemic circulation.
clips.narration: The left ventricle is much thicker, often ten to fifteen millimeters, because it must pump blood through the entire systemic circuit against greater resistance.

clips.changeMeaning: Both highlights remain visible while the scale marker enlarges to prompt visual confirmation of the approximate three-to-one thickness ratio.
clips.narration: Use the scale marker to compare the walls. The left ventricular myocardium is roughly three times thicker than the right because it generates much higher systemic pressure.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Valve Function and Backflow Prevention
modules.description: Open and closed valve models demonstrate atrioventricular and semilunar valve function during ventricular filling and ejection.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Classify tricuspid and mitral valves as atrioventricular valves.
Classify pulmonary and aortic valves as semilunar valves.
State which valve group is open or closed during ventricular filling and ejection.
Explain how pressure-driven valve closure prevents backflow.
instructions: Observe the two valve categories first.
Advance to compare open and closed states during filling and ejection.
Use the phase label to connect valve state with direction of blood flow.

components.text: Valve states

AV: tricuspid + mitral
Semilunar: pulmonary + aortic

clips.changeMeaning: Two highlight groups appear over atrioventricular and semilunar valve pairs, organizing the four valves by position and function.
clips.narration: The tricuspid and mitral valves are atrioventricular valves, located between atria and ventricles. The pulmonary and aortic valves are semilunar valves, located at the ventricular outflow tracts.

components.text:
Ventricular filling:
AV OPEN • Semilunar CLOSED

clips.changeMeaning: Open AV valves and closed semilunar valves show ventricular filling while preventing backflow from arteries.
clips.narration: During ventricular relaxation and filling, atrioventricular valves are open so blood can move from atria to ventricles. Semilunar valves are closed to prevent arterial backflow into the ventricles.

components.text:
Ventricular ejection:
AV CLOSED • Semilunar OPEN

clips.changeMeaning: The models swap to closed AV valves and open semilunar valves, showing ejection without backflow into the atria.
clips.narration: During ventricular contraction, atrioventricular valves close to prevent backflow into atria. Semilunar valves open so blood can exit into the pulmonary trunk and aorta.

components.text:
Core function:
prevent backflow

clips.changeMeaning: Both valve category highlights brighten to reinforce that leaflet closure maintains one-way blood flow through the heart.
clips.narration: Valves make the heart a one-way pump. Leaflets open when pressure drives blood forward and close when pressure would push blood backward.

modules.description: An unlabeled cutaway heart highlights structures while answer choices and feedback support active identification practice.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify unlabeled chambers, valves, and vessels on a cutaway heart.
Use anatomical relationships to distinguish similar structures.
Reinforce heart vocabulary with immediate feedback.
instructions: Say your answer before advancing to feedback.
Compare your choice with the highlighted location.
Use feedback to refine your mental map of the heart.

components.text: Which structure is highlighted?

A. Right atrium
B. Left ventricle
C. Aortic valve
D. Pulmonary veins
Advance for feedback.
Question 1: Which chamber is highlighted?

clips.changeMeaning: The teaching labels are removed, leaving only a highlighted structure and answer choices to shift from recognition to retrieval.
clips.narration: Now practice identifying structures without labels. Say the answer before you advance to the feedback.

components.text:
Answer: A. Right atrium
Clue: receives SVC and IVC blood.

clips.changeMeaning: Feedback confirms the right atrium and explains that venous inflow from the venae cavae helps identify it.
clips.narration: The correct answer is right atrium. It is on the patient's right side and receives systemic venous blood from the superior and inferior vena cava.

components.text:
A. Mitral valve
B. Tricuspid valve
C. Aortic valve
D. Pulmonary valve
Choose before advancing.

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves to the right atrioventricular valve location and the answer choices update to focus on valve identification.
clips.narration: Next question. Which valve lies between the right atrium and the right ventricle?

components.text:
Answer: B. Tricuspid valve
Right atrium → right ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: Feedback names the tricuspid valve and restates its chamber boundaries to support relationship-based identification.
clips.narration: The correct answer is tricuspid valve. It separates the right atrium from the right ventricle.

components.text:
A. Aorta
B. Superior vena cava
C. Pulmonary veins
D. Inferior vena cava

Answer: A. Aorta
Systemic outflow from left ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves to the great vessel leaving the left ventricle and feedback identifies it as the systemic outflow artery.
clips.narration: The highlighted great vessel is the aorta. It receives oxygenated blood from the left ventricle and distributes it to systemic circulation.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8: Blood Flow Tracing Quiz and Recap
modules.description: Students predict the next structure in blood flow, address pulmonary artery and vein exceptions, and finish with a final recap of core concepts.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict the next structure in the cardiac circulation pathway.
Distinguish pulmonary arteries from pulmonary veins by direction and oxygenation status.
Summarize the lab's core concepts: structural inventory, dual circuits, complete pathway, wall thickness, and valve function.
instructions: Say the next structure before revealing feedback.
Pay special attention to pulmonary arteries and veins, which are common points of confusion.
Use the recap as a final study checklist.

components.text:
Blood is in the right atrium.
What comes next?

A. Tricuspid valve
B. Pulmonary veins
C. Aortic valve
D. Left atrium

Recap:
1. Chambers, valves, vessels
2. Pulmonary + systemic circuits
3. Full blood path
4. LV wall thicker than RV
5. Valves prevent backflow
Right atrium → ?

A. Tricuspid valve  ✓
B. Pulmonary veins
C. Aortic valve
D. Left atrium

clips.changeMeaning: The quiz begins with the marker in the right atrium and asks for the next structure to prompt active recall of the pathway.
clips.narration: Blood has just entered the right atrium. The next structure is the tricuspid valve, leading into the right ventricle.

components.text: Right ventricle → pulmonary valve → ?

A. Pulmonary veins
B. Aorta
C. Pulmonary arteries  ✓
D. Inferior vena cava

clips.changeMeaning: The cell moves to the pulmonary outflow tract and the choices emphasize that pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the heart.
clips.narration: After the right ventricle, blood exits through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries. Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

components.text: Lungs → ? → Left atrium

A. Superior vena cava
B. Pulmonary veins  ✓
C. Pulmonary arteries
D. Aortic valve

clips.changeMeaning: The cell turns red at pulmonary venous return, reinforcing that pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood back to the left atrium.
clips.narration: After gas exchange in the lungs, oxygenated blood returns to the heart through pulmonary veins and enters the left atrium.

components.text: Left ventricle → aortic valve → ?

A. Aorta  ✓
B. Pulmonary trunk
C. Right atrium
D. Inferior vena cava

clips.changeMeaning: The red cell advances toward systemic outflow, asking learners to identify the vessel that receives blood from the left ventricle.
clips.narration: From the left atrium, blood crosses the mitral valve, enters the left ventricle, and exits through the aortic valve into the aorta.

components.text: Final study checklist

clips.changeMeaning: The quiz display transitions to a recap panel listing the five major concept areas for final consolidation and exam review.
clips.narration: To recap: you identified chambers, valves, and vessels; distinguished pulmonary and systemic circuits; traced the full blood path; related left ventricular wall thickness to systemic pressure; and explained how valves prevent backflow.
